headline: After a rough start, Commanders’ new coordinator has the defense taking charge
author: Tashan Reed

paragraphs.text: With more Washington Commanders bearing down on him than the New York Giants could possibly block, quarterback J.J. McCarthy had no choice but to chuck the ball downfield. The pass ended up near its intended target — but cornerback Rasul Douglas was right there to make the interception and seal the 24-21 win Nov. 12.

The Commanders’ defense dictated the terms of engagement. They play a sport where it’s widely accepted that the offense forces the defense to react, but they came into this season aiming to flip that notion on its head.

“It’s really a privilege to be able to play offense on the defensive side of the ball,” outside linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson said before the season. “You dictate what plays you’re going to see on the offense.”

To start the year, however, Washington’s defense was reeling. Through the first five games, the Commanders gave up 29.8 points per game (30th). Even after General Manager Adam Peters invested a stockpile of resources on that side of the ball and defensive coordinator Daronte Jones introduced a new scheme, they looked helpless.

Then, suddenly, everything changed. The defense morphed into an aggressive, attacking, playmaking unit. Since their narrow Week 6 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, they’ve allowed just 18.5 points per game (tied for eighth).

“One thing that happened in that game — and it kind of led over to the others a little bit — is the belief of the guys,” Jones told The Washington Post. “That’s a huge attribute that can go unnoticed if you’re not paying attention. It has to be our ability as coaches to piggyback on that belief and ask more of our guys.”

Jones’s scheme has played a major part in that turnaround. He heavily utilizes deception. He constantly works in disguised coverages, simulated pressures and exotic blitzes. He substitutes players frequently and deploys unique alignments along the defensive front and in the secondary. It’s all creating confusion and hesitation for offenses. When that happens, mistakes tend to follow.

The Commanders’ defense isn’t perfect, but it’s much closer to what it set out to be. That’s happened despite Washington losing defensive tackles Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw and linebacker Leo Chenal to season-ending injuries.

They’ll face their toughest challenge of the season when Washington (3-5-1) hosts the Cincinnati Bengals (7-2) on Monday. Quarterback Joe Burrow and wide receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins lead arguably the best offense in the NFL.
That doesn’t intimidate the Commanders.
“They feel like they can play with anybody,” Jones said. “That leads into, ‘Okay, in that case, we can do this, we can be that, we can move forward from here, we can continue to grow from here.’”
‘Hard for them, easy for us’

Across a decade as an NFL assistant with four different franchises, Jones has learned from different coaches. None had a greater influence than Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores, under whom Jones worked as the defensive backs coach from 2023-25. His biggest takeaway: Learning how to think outside the box.

“We’ve been trained almost in this profession to think of rules and not going outside of the norms,” Jones said. “And Flo, his courage to not even be in the box, right? There’s no box with him at all. You don’t know what thought he may come up with.”

When Commanders Coach Dan Quinn interviewed Jones this offseason, he was impressed by his forward-thinking mindset. Among Jones’s core principles was forcing offenses to adjust to the defense — often through pre-snap manipulation.

“He’s on the front edge of some things,” Quinn said in August. “Often at the line of scrimmage, offenses can have the pen last … What I like in the system that we have now is we are also into some of the checking to make the offense have to adjust.”

The deception game continues after the snap. A strategy Jones frequently uses is disguised coverages. There are times when it looks like the Commanders are playing man coverage but they’re actually playing zone and vice versa. On other plays, Washington will have players appear like they’re about to blitz before dropping back into coverage.
“It’s hard for them, easy for us,” linebacker Sonny Styles said.

Jones also often uses simulated pressures. On those plays, traditional pass rushers (such as defensive tackles) drop back into coverage while nontraditional pass rushers (such as cornerbacks) are sent on blitzes.
“It’s giving the offense a lot to think about in a short amount of time,” defensive end Charles Omenihu said. “They have to snap the ball and decipher after the snap. It can be difficult.”

The Commanders blitz a lot. Nobody blitzes as often as Flores — the Vikings blitz on an absurd 69.2 percent of their opponents’ drop backs — but Jones outpaces most defensive play callers. Washington has blitzed on 40.4 percent of opponents’ drop backs (third).

“Who made that rule to say four-down [defense] is a four-man rush and if you bring five, that’s a blitz?” Jones said. “When you think that, it’s like, ‘Well, five, six, they’re just numbers at the end of the day.’”
There are a lot of moving parts in Jones’s scheme. That complexity can easily lead to confusion throughout the defense, which defeats the purpose. Having strong communication is paramount.
Players credited Jones for his ability to teach effectively in the offseason, but there’s no replicating in-game action.

“We’re not asking guys to just be plug-and-play players,” Jones said. “Just to say, ‘Hey, this guy can be that in this scheme,’ well, no, he can’t. Everyone learns differently. And so, you can only move as fast as the slowest learner or the guy who’s the furthest behind because we’ve got to all move in one direction.”

Additionally, Jones had to be adaptable. He cut things within the scheme that weren’t working. When Washington hired longtime NFL coach Steve Wilks as a consultant during its Week 7 bye, Jones accepted his game-planning help.

“Honestly, that level of thinking of what you’re asking the players has to be what you are asking everyone,” Jones said. “So the open-mindedness of players and staff allows that thought process to grow.”
‘Comfortable being uncomfortable’
During the Commanders’ recent success, the structure of the defensive approach hasn’t changed much. Their early struggles didn’t lead them to abandon their principles.

Through the first games of the season, they blitzed on 43.2 percent of opponents’ drop backs (second), used a nickel package on 53 percent of their snaps (22nd) and played zone coverage on 76 percent of opponents’ drop backs (16th). Since then, they’ve blitzed on 36.6 percent of opponents’ drop backs (fifth), used nickel on 57.5 percent of their snaps (22nd) and played zone coverage on 80.1 percent of opponents’ drop backs (11th).

The biggest change: The Commanders have used 3-4 fronts less frequently. In the first five games, they used a 3-4 front on 34.9 percent of their defensive snaps. That’s down to just 17 percent since, but that’s largely because they have less depth at defensive tackle after losing Kinlaw and Payne.
For Washington, the real difference is the execution. The Commanders have stepped up in more key moments, limiting explosive plays and creating turnovers.

Through the first five games of the season, they allowed opponents to convert 43.3 percent of their third downs (24th), gave up touchdowns on 83.3 percent of their red zone possessions (last) and forced turnovers on just 3.4 percent of their drives (31st). Since then, they’ve allowed a 34.5 percent conversion rate on third downs (10th), given up touchdowns on 57.1 percent of their red zone possessions (14th) and forced turnovers on 11.4 percent of their drives (tied for 16th).

“If you get comfortable being uncomfortable in practice and in the meeting rooms, it starts to breed a level of confidence, right?” Jones said. “Now, that uncomfortable feeling becomes confidence. And then that confidence is what allows you to be able to execute on game day.”

There are still areas where the Commanders are leaving plenty to be desired. They’re generating a pressure rate of just 33.5 percent (24th) and a sack rate of 5.1 percent (26th). They’ve allowed opponents to convert 83.3 percent of their fourth downs (tied for 30th). Although the defense has become more reliable, it still has work to do.

“The sky’s the limit as long as we continue to progress and guys continue to stay grounded and continue to focus on the keys of playing great defense as a unit and togetherness,” Jones said. “As long as that happens, these guys can accomplish whatever they set their mind to.”
